question: Various types of speed detectors are used on Europe’s main roads, including speed cameras and average speed cameras. In Italy, these devices are also used on secondary and municipal roads, with all proceeds from fines going to the competent local authority.

Strategic positioning of speed detectors can create significant revenue for the public authorities, and has resulted in a situation where their main purpose no longer seems to be road safety, but rather to generate income for the authorities concerned. This practice has driven citizens to distraction, resulting in a series of acts of vandalism.

A clear case in point is that of Veneto, where eight speed detectors have been damaged in the last few months. It is widely believed that speed cameras are being used en masse as an oppressive means of ‘raking it in’, something that is undermining confidence in the institutions.

It is important to remember that the EU Treaties guarantee the free movement of goods and people on its roads, and that this principle cannot be undermined by practices whose only goal is to generate profit. In the light of the above: 1.

What is the Commission’s view of the way in which speed detectors are being used and positioned, and does it agree that it is necessary to have EU type approval rules and periodic checks for electronic speed detection devices?
What steps will it take to standardise automatic speed detection practices across the EU?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (25.7.2024) 1. The report on the application of the Directive (EU) 2015/413 (cross-border exchange - CBE Directive)1 found no cross-border cases where the evidence produced by automatic checking equipment was refused or not recognised because of the equipment unreliability.
Thus, harmonising detection methods was seen as non-justified interference in Member States’ enforcement policy choices.

Annex to this report provides a general example of effective deployment and operation of automatic checking equipment for detection of road traffic offences, according to which automatic checking equipment, in particular speed cameras, should be installed in places selected via a specific assessment. 2.

Stakeholder consultations for the proposal amending the CBE Directive2 showed that stakeholders perceived the intensity and methods concerning the detection of road traffic offences as the competence of Member States authorities. Moreover, the Measuring Instruments Directive 2014/32/EU3 does not cover cameras measuring speed or any other equipment used for enforcement of road traffic rules.

This Directive is currently subject to an ongoing evaluation, the results of which, including on the whether the equipment used for the detection of road traffic offences should be covered, are expected at the beginning of 2025.

However, any potential EU legal provisions on operation, design and performance, or methods of use, of such measuring equipment, would first require adoption of rules on its categorisation and standardisation, and setting up relevant conformity assessment procedures.
1 Directive (EU) 2015/413 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 March 2015 facilitating cross-

border exchange of information on road-safety-related traffic offences, OJ L 68, 13.3.2015, p. 9–25. Report to the European Parliament and the Council on the application of Directive (EU) 2015/413 facilitating cross-border exchange of information on road-safety-related traffic offences1 (‘CBE Directive’), COM (2016) 744 final. 2 COM/2023/126 final.
3 Directive 2014/32/EU on the harmonisation of the laws of the Member States relating to the making available on the market of measuring instruments, OJ L 96, 29.3.2014, p. 236.
